Le mois dernier, le président américain,: Last month, U.S. President Joe Biden announced the complete withdrawal of American troops from Afghanistan by August 31, 2021. On August 15, 2021, Kabul, the capital, fell to the Taliban, who now control the country. Since then, the question of defending Afghan women has become omnipresent. In the face of this reality, Afghan women shared their concerns and experiences with us.
Safia Hashimi déplore l'image stigmatisa: Safia Hashimi decries the stigmatizing image of Afghan women and the Afghan people conveyed in the media. Photo: courtesy of Safia Hashimi[/caption]
« Nous, les femmes afghanes, sommes capa: “We Afghan women are capable of so much. I don’t want what’s happening in my country right now to define me as a person,” says Safia Hashimi, who has lived in Montréal for five and a half years. “The way the media talk about Afghan women affects me, because it gives a bad image of Afghanistan,” she adds, referring to how their situation under Taliban rule is presented. She is outraged by Western media coverage of events in her country of origin, coverage she sometimes finds stigmatizing and dehumanizing. “One journalist said the Taliban had asked her to stand with the women, separated from the men.
La façon dont elle l’a présenté m’a mise: The way she presented it made me uncomfortable,” explains Ms. Hashimi, referring to a report aired on a major American network. “Elsewhere, there may be some discomfort with separating the genders, but in Afghanistan, it’s normal. In my opinion, that cultural difference was exaggerated,” she says. She is also tired of the clichés that depict her country as a land of refugees, war and violence. Regarding the media coverage and the discourse centred on the urgency of “saving Afghan women,” which is so common in the West, Ms. Hashimi points out that many Afghan women are already mobilized around this issue.
Elle cite plusieurs d’entre elles, souve: She names several of them, often little known, who have fought for justice: for example, Queen Soraya Tarzi, who fought for women’s rights alongside her husband, and Rula Ghani, the wife of the last president, who fought for the rights of women, children and refugees. “Women will rise up to fight the injustices of the current government. They’ll try to silence us, but it will never work,” she says firmly. “We have hope for a free future and we will never yield to tyranny!”
Mari Nazari, qui vit également à Montréa: Mari Nazari, who also lives in Montréal, shares this view. “As an Afghan woman myself, I fundamentally believe that Afghan women are very strong. So talk like ‘We have to save the Afghan woman’ makes me uncomfortable,” says the master’s student in career counselling. “Unfortunately, society and the Taliban government don’t let women express their strength. I’d also like for our dear Afghan women to be given a bit of credit.” She is proud to be Afghan, but that pride comes with its share of worries.
« Ça ne doit pas être facile, me dit-on: “‘It can’t be easy,’ I’m told,” she says, describing the microaggressions she experiences. Drawing on her own experiences, Ms. Nazari uses her voice on social media to raise awareness about the issues facing the Afghan people. Awareness is increasingly important. But for the student, empathy is not enough. “I find it really frustrating that people don’t ask me any questions about the causes of the current situation in Afghanistan. Because my country hasn’t always been like this,” she adds, frustrated. “I don’t see any reaction other than empathy. There needs to be action, too. I want more real awareness,” she insists.
Le discours actuel sur les Afghanes affe: The current discourse on Afghan women affects Muslim women of many backgrounds. These concerns led Hiba J. to post a video on Instagram addressing these issues. She hesitated a great deal before doing so. “I didn’t want to impose myself on what’s happening in Afghanistan and on the efforts of Afghan activists,” explains the activist of Moroccan origin. “The discourse has become simplistic, presenting these women as oppressed people who cover up against their will, when the problem is much broader, with many other nuances that we forget to mention,” laments the activist with Béliers solidaires, a collective formed by students and former students of École Henri-Bourassa to denounce hatred. This type of discourse stings the young woman, who wears the hijab.
Elle y entend des parallèles avec les pr: She hears parallels with the statements surrounding Bill 21. “The same rhetoric was used, even though I’m not Afghan,” she explains. “The argument that always comes up to defend this law is that these women are oppressed. And that it’s up to Quebec to save them by taking off their veils. As if we had no choice.” Rukaya Achhal, a history student at Université de Montréal, finds the discourse on how Afghan women dress particularly troubling.
« On associe l’image de femmes plus vêtu: “Women who are more covered up are associated with a regression in women’s rights. And there’s this unhealthy obsession with Afghan women of the 1970s, who wore very Western-style skirts,” says the student, who is of Moroccan origin. “There are dubious parallels being drawn, for example, as I was saying, the idea that a woman who is more covered up, who wears traditional clothing associated with Islam, means a step backward.” “In the media, there’s little room for Muslim women to speak on this kind of issue, even though they’re the ones most affected,” Ms. Achhal laments. She feels that Bill 21 portrays her as submissive. “I chose to wear the hijab to keep my boundaries with my body, and I chose to have a relationship with my spirituality that I consider healthy by wearing these clothes,” she says firmly and with conviction. Ms. Achhal finds it hypocritical for governments like those of Quebec and France to criticize other regimes for trampling on Muslim women’s rights, given that these governments can themselves be the target of similar criticism.
« Quand on interdit aux musulmanes le dr: “When Muslim women are banned from wearing the hijab, you indirectly cut off their access to many opportunities. You ask them to choose between their faith and their access to work and education. And nobody talks about that,” the student observes. She acknowledges that there is real danger to Afghan women’s rights under the Taliban regime, which jeopardizes their access to education and the labour market, but says that danger is just as real here.
Amira Bennani*, porte-parole de Femmes m: Amira Bennani*, spokesperson for Femmes musulmanes du Québec (FMQ), a group of Muslim decolonial feminists, holds the same position. In her view, the fight against the Taliban does not preclude the fight against the Islamophobia that Afghanistan suffers from. “Westerners are instrumentalizing Afghan women and their religion to justify their interventions,” says Ms. Bennani.
Elle croit aussi qu’il faut faire confia: She also believes that the people themselves must be trusted to fight these problems, because they know their reality best.
Amina Jamal, professeure à l’université: Amina Jamal, a professor at Ryerson University, is a sociologist who specializes in South Asian feminism. The researcher stresses that it is important to understand the context in which the latest developments in Afghanistan took place. She goes back to 1979, <l1>the start of the U.S.-Soviet war.</l1> “Under the Soviet-backed government at the time, Afghan women had more rights than before, and far more than elsewhere in South Asia,” the professor recalls.
Elle explique qu’à cette époque, les Éta: She explains that at that time, the United States intervened to fight Soviet communism, supporting conservative groups like the Taliban. “There are photos of meetings between the American president of the day, Ronald Reagan, and the Taliban, as well as photos of Taliban members with representatives of American oil companies. These facts are usually rarely discussed today,” explains the Ryerson University researcher. For the professor, the feminist humanitarian justification for interventions in Afghanistan stems from a colonial logic. “Researchers call this kind of discourse ‘colonizing discourse,’ because its aim is to show that the West is the land of freedom and that Islam is the land of the oppressed,” the researcher explains. “Foreign interventions aren’t really meant to liberate Afghan women, but rather to turn them into clones of Western women.
Et nous savons que ça ne fonctionne pas: And we know that doesn’t work,” she says. She believes that the Islamophobia surrounding the question of Afghan women comes from a misunderstanding of sharia, which is often misinterpreted by non-Muslims. Sharia is not a legal code, but a set of principles that govern justice, equality and compassion.
Les différentes sociétés sont libres de: Different societies are free to practise these principles according to their own interpretations and circumstances. “The Taliban’s sharia is a particular version based on Wahhabism and Salafism, which is embedded in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It’s false to say that the Taliban’s sharia is Islam,” Ms. Jamal clarifies, adding that the Quran contains many feminist teachings.

Le soir du 20 août 2021, à l’appel du Ce: On the evening of August 20, 2021, at the call of the Centre des femmes afghanes de Montréal, many women came to testify to the strength they show in the face of extremist regimes. Gathered at Dorchester Square, several spoke to share their perspectives, as the Afghan national anthem boomed from the loudspeakers and the tricolour flag was held high. Queenm Malika, her makeup in the colours of her country, stepped onto the stage. “My childhood in Afghanistan counts for me among the best moments of my life,” she told us afterward.
C’est la situation politique qui a forcé: It was the political situation that forced her family to leave the country. “After immigrating, I quickly understood that systemic racism was very present. You can see it.”
Mme Malika est particulièrement critique: Ms. Malika is particularly critical of the motives of the foreign nations intervening in her country of origin. Like many, she doesn’t believe in the stated reason of <l1>humanitarian intervention in Afghanistan for women’s rights</l1>, citing the major feminist reforms introduced by the Afghan queen Soraya Tarzi in the 1920s, long before similar reforms were carried out in many Western countries. “And to think they want to come here to teach us how to be Muslims!” she exclaims.
L’activiste demande aux nations étrangèr: The activist asks foreign nations to leave her country alone, a request also made by many other Afghan women at the event. While she condemns the Taliban regime, she is just as critical of the previous government which, in her view, was imposed on the Afghan people by outside forces. And this imposition, she believes, is part of the long series of colonialist interventions Afghanistan has endured throughout history, whether by the Greeks, the Persians, the Mongols, or the British, the Soviets and the Americans. “They took away all women’s rights to subjugate them.
Parce que les femmes afghanes se battent: Because Afghan women fight back,” she believes. She is extremely worried that the situation will happen again. She firmly believes in her own people’s ability to rebuild their country. “The others need to stop sticking their noses into our business and give us time to build our country. And then we’ll work with them on our own terms.”
Il y a quelques années, Queenm Malika pr: A few years ago, Queenm Malika took part in this reconstruction effort. She returned to her country several times as a freelance journalist, with the mission of combatting the disinformation surrounding Afghan geopolitics. There, she interviewed several political actors, including Taliban members, and members of several of the ethnic groups that make up the Afghan people.
Aujourd’hui, la mère de famille souhaite: Today, the mother of a family wants to go back to university to study political science and change things for immigrants like her, here in Quebec. Twenty years after the start of their military intervention in Afghanistan, American troops bowed out this Monday. Yet the discourse surrounding the fate of Afghan women continues, and the Taliban’s control is spreading across the country. For many Afghan and Muslim women, once again, there is one great absence in all of this: context.
